analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $9.50 and ties future increases to congressional pay raises.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to committee in December 2007, drew no cosponsors, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stepped the federal minimum wage up to $8.00, then $8.75, then $9.50 an hour by mid-2011 [S2]. After that, every July the minimum wage would automatically rise by the same percentage as any pay raise members of Congress receive [S2] [S3]. The idea was that minimum wage workers' pay should move in step with the pay of the officials who set it [S3]. It was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor issues and never moved further [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the millions of workers earning near the federal minimum, who would see their hourly pay rise in three scheduled steps and then rise automatically whenever Congress votes itself a pay increase [S2] [S3]. Workers whose wages hover slightly above the minimum would also gain as pay scales shift upward.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps: $8.00 on January 1, 2010, $8.75 on October 1, 2010, and $9.50 on July 1, 2011 [S2] [S3].

Beginning July 1, 2012, and each July thereafter, the minimum wage would automatically increase by the same percentage as any annual pay adjustment Members of Congress receive, ending the need for Congress to pass a new minimum wage bill each time [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum wage, especially restaurants, retail stores, and other low-wage service businesses, would face higher payroll costs. Some of that cost would likely reach consumers through higher prices, and some economists argue employers respond by reducing hiring or hours for the least experienced workers.

drawbacks.text: The scheduled increases would raise labor costs for small businesses and low-margin employers in lower-cost regions, where a $9.50 federal wage exceeds prevailing wages; good-faith opponents argue this can reduce entry-level hiring or hours.

Tying the minimum wage to congressional pay raises is an unusual formula; if Congress ever voted itself a large pay increase, the minimum wage would jump by the same percentage regardless of economic conditions, and if Congress froze its own pay, the minimum wage would freeze too.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is straightforward: a higher, then automatically adjusted wage floor for the lowest-paid workers, which would lift incomes for millions of households [S2] [S3]. The cost is higher payroll expenses for employers of low-wage labor, with the usual contested questions about effects on hiring, hours, and prices. The congressional-pay indexing mechanism is a mixed design: it removes the politics from future raises, but it also means the wage floor rises or freezes for reasons unrelated to the economy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 18, 2007, referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton introduced the bill in the Senate on December 18, 2007, with Senator Reid introducing it on her behalf [S3] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; no further action was taken for the remainder of the Congress [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum wage labor were better off, since wages stayed where the 2007 minimum wage law had set them and no higher indexed floor was created. Members of Congress were also spared a mechanism that would have automatically tied their pay raises to raises for the lowest-paid workers. Minimum wage workers gained nothing from this bill, though a separate 2007 law had already scheduled increases to $7.25 by mid-2009.

for.name: Sen. Hillary Rodham Clinton
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the minimum wage to $9.50 and index future increases to congressional pay raises; the Senate majority leader introduced it on her behalf while she was campaigning for president.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no action; no hearing, markup, or vote occurred, so the bill died in committee.

against.name: U.S. Senate
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee and never took it up; no senator cosponsored it during the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Democratic-sponsored proposal with no Republican or other cosponsors, and with a Democratic-controlled Senate taking no action on it, the record shows no bipartisan coalition behind it [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have raised their payroll costs by moving the federal wage floor to $9.50 and then indexing it. Their interest in blocking it ran against the wage gains the bill offered low-paid workers.

industries.industry: Members of Congress (as a pay-receiving class)
industries.note: The bill would have tied the minimum wage to their own pay adjustments, raising the political cost of any future congressional pay raise and removing their discretion to raise their pay without also raising the wage floor. It did not reduce their pay itself.
